title: Mark–recapture of hedgerow snails
stem: Ecologists estimated the population size of a land snail in three hedgerows using capture–mark–release–recapture. On day 1 snails were collected for 30 minutes, marked with a dot of non-toxic paint on the shell and released at the point of capture. Two days later a second 30-minute sample was collected from the same hedgerow.

data.caption: Numbers of snails captured, marked and recaptured in three hedgerows

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the estimated population size of snails in hedgerow A, using the Lincoln index.
markscheme: 400 (snails)
parts.notes: Award 1 mark if the numbers are substituted correctly but the arithmetic is wrong.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce, with a reason, which hedgerow gives the least reliable population estimate.
markscheme: hedgerow C
smallest number of recaptured/marked snails in second sample (only 6)
a change of one or two recaptures would change the estimate greatly / estimate very sensitive to chance
(so) large uncertainty in estimate of about 1230 snails
parts.notes: Mark for hedgerow C only awarded with a valid reason.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State two assumptions that must be true for the Lincoln index to give an accurate estimate.
markscheme: marked snails mix randomly/fully with the unmarked population before resampling
no births/deaths/immigration/emigration between samples / closed population
marks are not lost/rubbed off between samples
marking does not affect survival/behaviour/chance of recapture (e.g. predators do not notice paint)
all individuals have an equal chance of being captured

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how the population estimate would be affected if some of the paint marks wore off between day 1 and day 3.
markscheme: fewer marked snails are recognised/counted in the second sample
denominator (recaptures) smaller so population size is overestimated
Allow: some marked snails counted as unmarked

title: Energy flow in a reed-bed wetland
stem: The energy available at each trophic level of a freshwater reed-bed food chain was estimated over one year. Values for producers are net primary production.

data.caption: Energy available at each trophic level of a reed-bed ecosystem

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer from producers to primary consumers.
parts.notes: Answer must be expressed as a percentage; 0.088 alone scores 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why only a small proportion of the energy in primary consumers is available to secondary consumers.
markscheme: energy released in cell respiration is lost as heat (from the ecosystem)
not all of the primary consumers are eaten (some die and go to decomposers)
not all parts eaten are digested/absorbed / energy lost in faeces/egestion
energy lost in excretion/urea
energy used for movement/maintenance (ultimately lost as heat)
heat cannot be converted back to chemical energy / energy cannot be recycled

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage of the producers' energy that reaches the tertiary consumers.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest, using the data, why this food chain does not have a fifth trophic level.
markscheme: only 14 kJ m⁻² y⁻¹ available at tertiary level
with about 7–10 % transfer a fifth level would receive only about 1 kJ m⁻² y⁻¹
too little energy to support a viable population (of large predators) / OWTTE
large home range/area would be needed to obtain enough energy

title: A candidate inhibitor of a bacterial enzyme
stem: A pharmaceutical team tested compound X as a possible inhibitor of a bacterial enzyme. Initial reaction rates were measured at five substrate concentrations with and without 0.5 mmol dm⁻³ compound X at 30 °C and pH 7.0 (n = 5 for each mean).

data.caption: Initial rate of reaction with and without compound X

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage decrease in the rate of reaction caused by compound X at a substrate concentration of 5 mmol dm⁻³.
markscheme: 47.2 % (decrease)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Analyse the standard deviations to determine whether compound X has a significant effect at 20 mmol dm⁻³.
markscheme: ranges overlap: 45.0–51.2 and 41.2–48.0 µmol min⁻¹ / means differ by less than the SDs
difference (3.5 µmol min⁻¹) probably not significant at 20 mmol dm⁻³
in contrast, at 1–5 mmol dm⁻³ the SD ranges do not overlap / effect clear at low substrate concentration
a statistical test (e.g. t-test) would be needed to confirm

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Deduce, with a reason, whether compound X is a competitive or a non-competitive inhibitor.
markscheme: competitive
inhibition is overcome/reduced at high substrate concentration
rate with X approaches the same maximum rate (Vmax) as without X
parts.notes: No mark for 'competitive' without a reason based on the data.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how a competitive inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction.
markscheme: inhibitor has a similar shape/chemical structure to the substrate
binds (reversibly) to the active site
prevents substrate binding / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes formed
inhibitor and substrate compete for active sites
increasing substrate concentration increases chance of substrate rather than inhibitor colliding with active site

title: Antibody response to a two-dose vaccine
stem: Volunteers (n = 24) received a new vaccine against a respiratory virus on day 0 and a second dose on day 28. The concentration of virus-specific antibody in their blood plasma was measured.

data.caption: Mean plasma antibody concentration after vaccination

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the changes in mean antibody concentration between day 0 and day 28.
markscheme: increases from 2 to a peak of 64 arbitrary units
peak at (about) day 14
then falls to 40 arbitrary units by day 28
slow initial increase / little change in first 7 days
parts.notes: At least one quoted value with units for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage increase in mean antibody concentration between day 28 and day 35.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the difference between the response to the first dose and the response to the second dose.
markscheme: second response faster and larger / higher concentration reached sooner
first dose: antigen activates specific B cells (with help from helper T cells) / clonal selection
memory cells are produced after the first dose
memory cells persist and recognise the antigen at the second dose
memory cells divide rapidly to form many plasma cells
plasma cells secrete large amounts of antibody

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest one reason for the large standard deviations on days 35 and 42.
markscheme: individual variation in immune response (age/health/genotype)
some volunteers may have had previous exposure to the virus
differences in timing of sampling / Allow: SD increases as the mean increases

title: Limiting factors in a tomato glasshouse
stem: A grower measured the rate of photosynthesis of tomato plants in a glasshouse at increasing light intensities, at two carbon dioxide concentrations. At 400 ppm CO₂ the rate rose and then levelled off at 18 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹; at 1000 ppm CO₂ it levelled off at 29 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline what is meant by a limiting factor in photosynthesis.
markscheme: the factor that is furthest from its optimum / in shortest supply
it determines the rate of photosynthesis
increasing it increases the rate (until another factor becomes limiting)
Allow named examples: light intensity, CO₂ concentration, temperature

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis at 400 ppm CO₂ levels off at high light intensity.
markscheme: light is no longer the limiting factor
CO₂ concentration (or temperature) is now limiting
the rate of carbon fixation (by Rubisco) cannot increase further
evidence: rate increases further at 1000 ppm CO₂

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suggest two reasons why the grower might not raise the CO₂ concentration above 1000 ppm.
markscheme: another factor (light/temperature) would become limiting so little extra yield
cost of CO₂ / heating outweighs the value of extra yield
high CO₂ may be unsafe for workers
stomata may close at very high CO₂ / OWTTE

title: Nerve impulses and synapses
stem: Motor neurons transmit impulses from the spinal cord to skeletal muscles.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the approximate resting potential of a neuron.
markscheme: −70 mV (Allow −60 to −80 mV; sign and unit required)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the resting potential is established and maintained.
markscheme: sodium–potassium pump uses ATP / active transport
pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in
membrane more permeable to K⁺ / K⁺ leaks out faster than Na⁺ leaks in
inside is negative relative to outside
negatively charged proteins/organic ions inside the axon

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Outline how myelination increases the speed of transmission along an axon.
markscheme: myelin insulates the axon / prevents ion movement across membrane
depolarisation only at nodes of Ranvier
impulse jumps from node to node / saltatory conduction
fewer depolarisations needed over a given distance

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A pesticide inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Predict, with a reason, the effect on a muscle supplied by a motor neuron.
markscheme: acetylcholine is not broken down / remains in the synaptic cleft
continues to bind receptors on the postsynaptic membrane / repeated depolarisation
muscle stays contracted / spasms / paralysis

title: Receptors for hormones
stem: Hormones act on target cells by binding to specific receptors. Oestradiol is a steroid hormone; adrenaline (epinephrine) is an amine hormone.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Distinguish between the receptors used by oestradiol and by adrenaline.
markscheme: oestradiol receptor intracellular (cytoplasm/nucleus) whereas adrenaline receptor in plasma membrane / transmembrane
oestradiol is hydrophobic/passes through membrane whereas adrenaline is hydrophilic/cannot cross membrane
oestradiol–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor/alters gene expression whereas adrenaline acts via a second messenger
parts.notes: Each point must give both sides of the distinction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Outline how binding of adrenaline to a G protein-coupled receptor leads to a response in a liver cell.
markscheme: adrenaline binds to receptor on the outer surface, changing receptor conformation
G protein activated / GDP replaced by GTP
(α subunit) activates adenylyl cyclase
cyclic AMP (second messenger) produced
cAMP activates protein kinase / phosphorylation cascade / amplification
glycogen broken down to glucose / glycogenolysis

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suggest why the same signalling molecule can cause different responses in different cell types.
markscheme: different cells have different receptor types for the same ligand
different signal transduction pathways/second messengers in different cells
different target proteins/enzymes/genes present depending on cell differentiation
Allow: example such as adrenaline causes vasoconstriction in some vessels but glycogen breakdown in liver

title: Cell respiration and ATP
stem: Cell respiration releases energy from organic molecules to produce ATP.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare and contrast anaerobic respiration in humans and in yeast.
markscheme: both: glycolysis in the cytoplasm
both: small yield of ATP / 2 ATP per glucose
both: no oxygen required
both: NAD regenerated so glycolysis can continue
humans produce lactate whereas yeast produce ethanol
yeast produce CO₂ whereas humans do not
lactate can be converted back (in liver) whereas ethanol is not reused by yeast / OWTTE
parts.notes: At least one similarity and one difference for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe how a simple respirometer can be used to measure the rate of aerobic respiration of germinating seeds.
markscheme: seeds in a sealed tube with an alkali (KOH/soda lime) to absorb CO₂
O₂ uptake reduces gas volume/pressure
coloured liquid moves along capillary tube towards the seeds
distance moved measured over a fixed time
volume = πr² × distance / rate as volume per unit time per gram
control tube with glass beads/dead seeds of equal volume
constant temperature / water bath

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how ATP is produced in mitochondria during aerobic respiration.
markscheme: pyruvate enters mitochondrion / link reaction in matrix
pyruvate decarboxylated and oxidised to an acetyl group / forms acetyl CoA, producing CO₂ and NADH
Krebs cycle: acetyl group combined with a 4C compound to form a 6C compound
decarboxylation and oxidation reactions release CO₂ and reduce NAD/FAD
one ATP formed per turn by substrate-level phosphorylation
NADH/FADH₂ donate electrons to the electron transport chain on the inner membrane/cristae
energy from electron flow used to pump protons into the intermembrane space
proton gradient formed across inner membrane
protons diffuse back through ATP synthase / chemiosmosis
ATP synthase phosphorylates ADP to ATP / oxidative phosphorylation
oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water with protons
parts.notes: Reject glycolysis details as they do not occur in mitochondria.

title: Populations, interactions and carbon
stem: Ecologists study how populations change and how matter cycles in ecosystems.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline how random quadrat sampling is used to estimate the population size of a plant species in a meadow.
markscheme: meadow mapped as a grid / measuring tapes as axes
random coordinates generated (random number table/generator)
quadrat of known area placed at each coordinate
number of individuals of the species counted in each quadrat
large number of quadrats / repeat to reduce error
mean per quadrat calculated
population = mean density × total area of meadow

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the processes by which carbon moves between organisms and the atmosphere.
markscheme: photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the atmosphere / producers fix carbon
carbon passed to consumers by feeding
cell respiration (by producers, consumers, decomposers) releases CO₂
decomposers/saprotrophs digest dead organic matter, releasing CO₂
combustion of biomass/fossil fuels releases CO₂
methanogenesis by archaea releases methane which is oxidised to CO₂
incomplete decomposition leads to peat/fossil fuel formation (carbon sink)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how interactions between species can regulate population sizes in a community.
markscheme: carrying capacity / populations limited by density-dependent factors
interspecific competition for a shared limited resource (food/light/space)
competition reduces growth/survival/reproduction of the weaker competitor
competitive exclusion may eliminate a species from an area
predation: more prey supports more predators
predators reduce prey numbers, then predator numbers fall (cycles)
predator–prey oscillations lag each other
herbivory limits plant populations / plants defended by toxins/spines
parasitism/pathogens spread faster at high density, reducing population
mutualism increases population of both species (e.g. mycorrhizae, pollination)
named example of any interaction with an effect on population size
parts.notes: Award marks for mechanisms, not for lists of interaction types.

title: Defence and coordination in the body
stem: The human body is protected against pathogens and coordinates its systems to respond to changing demands.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the role of blood clotting in defence against disease.
markscheme: damage to blood vessel / skin exposes collagen
platelets activated / release clotting factors
cascade of reactions / thrombin produced
thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin
fibrin forms a mesh trapping blood cells
clot seals wound, preventing entry of pathogens
also prevents blood loss

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Outline how B lymphocytes produce specific antibodies after infection.
markscheme: antigen presented by phagocyte/macrophage to helper T cell
B cell with complementary antibody/receptor binds the antigen
helper T cell activates this specific B cell
activated B cell divides by mitosis / clonal expansion
clone differentiates into plasma cells
plasma cells secrete specific antibodies
memory cells also formed

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how the nervous system integrates changes in ventilation rate and heart rate during vigorous exercise.
markscheme: increased cell respiration in muscles raises blood CO₂ concentration
CO₂ lowers blood pH
chemoreceptors in carotid arteries/aorta/medulla detect the fall in pH
impulses sent to the respiratory centre in the medulla (brainstem)
more frequent impulses to diaphragm and intercostal muscles
ventilation rate and depth increase, removing CO₂ and supplying O₂
cardiovascular centre in medulla also receives signals (chemoreceptors/baroreceptors)
sympathetic nerve impulses to the sinoatrial node increase heart rate
adrenaline secreted by adrenal glands also increases heart rate / endocrine input
more blood/oxygen delivered to muscles
parasympathetic (vagus) impulses slow heart rate after exercise / negative feedback
